chapter_summary:
Moving to the cloud, specifically to AWS, offers a compelling value proposition that extends far beyond mere technological upgrade. It fundamentally transforms how businesses operate, manage costs, and innovate. AWS highlights six key advantages that drive this value. The first is the ability to **trade capital expense for variable expense**. In traditional IT, you invest heavily in hardware, data centers, and infrastructure upfront (CapEx), often guessing your capacity needs. With AWS, you pay only for the compute, storage, and other resources you actually consume, turning CapEx into OpEx. This eliminates the need for large initial investments and allows for more predictable budgeting based on actual usage.

Secondly, you **benefit from massive economies of scale**. Because AWS operates at such an enormous scale, serving millions of customers globally, it can achieve lower per-unit costs for hardware, power, and cooling than any single company could on its own. These savings are then passed on to customers through lower prices. This means you get enterprise-grade infrastructure at a fraction of the cost. The third advantage is to **stop guessing capacity**. In on-premises environments, you often over-provision resources "just in case" to handle peak loads, leading to wasted capacity and costs. With AWS, you can provision exactly the amount of resources you need and scale up or down dynamically, eliminating the guesswork and ensuring you only pay for what's necessary.

The fourth advantage is a dramatic **increase in speed and agility**. Deploying new applications or services on-premises can take weeks or months to procure hardware, install software, and configure networks. With AWS, you can provision thousands of servers in minutes, experiment rapidly, and iterate on ideas much faster. This agility allows businesses to respond quickly to market changes and innovate at an accelerated pace. Closely related, the fifth advantage is to **stop spending money running and maintaining data centers**. Managing physical infrastructure, including power, cooling, security, and hardware maintenance, is a significant operational burden and cost center. AWS handles all of this for you, freeing up your IT staff to focus on higher-value activities that differentiate your business, rather than undifferentiated heavy lifting.

Finally, AWS allows you to **go global in minutes**. With its extensive global infrastructure, you can deploy your applications to multiple regions around the world with just a few clicks. This enables you to provide lower latency to your global customer base, comply with data residency requirements, and build highly resilient, geographically dispersed applications without the enormous investment of building physical data centers in each location. This global reach is a powerful enabler for businesses looking to expand internationally.

When considering a move to AWS, understanding **Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)** is crucial. TCO is a financial estimate intended to help buyers and owners determine the direct and indirect costs of a product or system. For cloud migration, a TCO analysis would compare the costs of running your applications on-premises versus on AWS. On-premises costs include hardware procurement, software licenses, data center space, power, cooling, network infrastructure, IT staff salaries, maintenance, and disaster recovery. AWS costs include compute, storage, networking, database services, and other service usage, along with potential support plans. While AWS eliminates many CapEx items, it introduces OpEx costs that need careful management. AWS provides a TCO Calculator to help estimate these savings by inputting your current infrastructure details.

A common mistake is assuming cloud is always cheaper without proper planning and optimization. While the potential for savings is immense, it's easy to incur unexpected costs if resources are left running unnecessarily, if services are over-provisioned, or if reserved instances or savings plans are not utilized for stable workloads. Another pitfall is neglecting the **Shared Responsibility Model**, where AWS is responsible for the *security of the cloud* (the underlying infrastructure), and you, the customer, are responsible for the *security in the cloud* (your data, applications, operating systems, network configuration, etc.). Misunderstanding this can lead to security vulnerabilities. Always remember that while AWS provides the secure foundation, you are responsible for configuring your resources securely. By leveraging AWS's cost management tools, rightsizing instances, and embracing automation, organizations can fully realize the economic and operational benefits of the AWS cloud.

screens.title: The AWS Cloud Value Proposition
screens.subtitle: Why organizations move from on-premises infrastructure to AWS and the six core advantages they gain

narration.text: In this short module we will explore why migrating workloads to AWS is more than a technology change — it’s an operational and economic transformation. You will learn the six core advantages that AWS offers: trading upfront capital expense for pay-as-you-go consumption, benefiting from massive economies of scale, avoiding capacity guessing, increasing speed and agility, removing the burden of running data centers, and the ability to go global rapidly. I’ll also guide you through how to think about Total Cost of Ownership for a migration, what costs to include, and the common pitfalls that lead teams to surprise bills. We will use a small, concrete scenario to practice identifying on-premises cost categories and mapping them to likely AWS services so you can present a simple TCO comparison. Along the way we’ll highlight common misconceptions, like assuming cloud is always cheaper, and emphasize the Shared Responsibility Model for security. By the end you should be able to explain each advantage, sketch a basic TCO comparison, and identify basic cost-management techniques. As you listen, notice which advantage matters most to your own organization and why.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: AWS shifts infrastructure from fixed capital investments to flexible, operational consumption while giving organizations scale, speed, and global reach — but realizing savings requires deliberate cost and security practices.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Practice
screens.subtitle: Use a small scenario to practice TCO mapping and cost-category identification

narration.text: This page sets an applied practice objective: you will translate a small on-premises deployment into likely AWS cost categories and list qualitative benefits beyond direct savings. Specifically, you will identify on-premises cost categories such as hardware amortization, software licenses, data center space and utilities, staff time, and backup solutions. Then you will map those to AWS equivalents: compute, storage, networking, managed databases, and support or operations costs. Finally, you will name at least three qualitative benefits of migration such as faster experimentation, simplified maintenance, and global reach. Practicing this mapping matters because it clarifies which costs disappear, which are transformed, and which remain as operational expenses. When presenting to management, a clear TCO comparison that includes non-monetary advantages is more persuasive than raw numbers alone. This exercise will prepare you to draft a short, defensible migration recommendation.

keyIdea.title: Practice objective
keyIdea.text: Translate a concrete on-premises setup into AWS service-based cost categories and articulate three non-monetary benefits.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Applied Practice
Practice Scenario
Your company runs a web application with:
5 physical servers (approx. m5.large each)
10 TB storage
One IT staff member spending 20% time
Annual costs:
  Hardware (amortized): $10,000
  Software licenses: $2,000
  Data center, power, cooling: $5,000
  IT staff cost (20% of $80,000): $16,000
  Backup/recovery: $3,000
Use this scenario to list on-premises cost categories and map them to AWS services such as compute, storage, and managed backup.
How to map costs
  • • Hardware amortization → Compute (EC2) and instance billing or managed compute alternatives.
  • • Storage and backups → Object or block storage services and snapshot/backup charges.
  • • Data center utilities → Eliminated by provider, replaced by service fees.
  • • Staff time → Shifts from maintenance to higher-value cloud operations and engineering.
  • • Software licenses → Either migrated, replaced by managed services, or continued as licenses hosted on cloud instances.
Key Takeaway

A simple scenario helps expose where costs move and which qualitative benefits to highlight, such as faster deployment and fewer maintenance tasks.

screens.title: Trade CapEx for OpEx
screens.subtitle: How shifting from upfront hardware purchases to pay-as-you-go changes budgeting and risk

narration.text: Trading capital expense for variable expense means you stop buying hardware up front and start paying for the resources you actually use. In traditional on-premises IT you absorb the cost and risk of buying servers, networking gear, and data center space, and then guess capacity needs. That guesswork often leads to either under-provisioning for peaks or over-provisioning and wasted capital. With AWS you move those fixed purchases into operational expense: monthly or hourly charges for compute, storage, and managed services. A concrete example is replacing an amortized server fleet with on-demand instances or reserved capacity. Instead of a ten-thousand-dollar hardware line item you may pay monthly for instances only when they run. This improves cash flow and reduces the risk of stranded assets. A common misconception is that OpEx is always more expensive; in fact, OpEx can be cheaper when you avoid over-provisioning and take advantage of elasticity and reserved pricing for predictable workloads. When you prepare a TCO comparison, include both the elimination of CapEx and the introduction of recurring service charges, and show how expected utilization changes the break-even point. To practice, imagine replacing five amortized servers with pay-as-you-go instances and show how monthly costs vary with utilization. What assumptions about utilization drive your recommendation?

keyIdea.title: Financial shift
keyIdea.text: Moving from CapEx to OpEx improves cash flow and reduces asset risk, but requires modeling utilization to show real savings.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › CapEx vs OpEx
Trade capital expense for variable expense
Stop buying and maintaining hardware up front; pay for what you use instead.
On-premises case
  • • Large upfront hardware purchases and capacity planning guesses.
  • • Costs include space, power, cooling, and hardware amortization.
AWS case
  • • Convert CapEx to OpEx with pay-for-use compute and storage.
  • • Use reserved or savings plans for predictable workloads to reduce OpEx.
Example
Five amortized servers become hourly instances. If utilization is low or variable, pay-as-you-go avoids wasted capital. If utilization is constant, reserved pricing can combine both OpEx predictability and lower rates.
Visual comparison
CapEx
Large up-front payment for hardware, depreciated over years, with risk of underuse.
OpEx
Ongoing service charges that align cost with actual consumption and allow faster changes.
Common misconception
Some assume OpEx always costs more. The truth is that OpEx reduces wasted capital when utilization fluctuates; success requires active rightsizing and use of savings mechanisms for steady state workloads.
Key Takeaway

Model utilization when converting CapEx to OpEx to see where pay-as-you-go buys flexibility and when reserved pricing is worthwhile.

screens.title: Massive Economies of Scale
screens.subtitle: How AWS's large scale reduces per-unit costs and benefits customers

narration.text: Economies of scale means larger providers can buy and operate resources more cheaply per unit than smaller organizations. In the context of cloud computing, AWS purchases hardware, builds efficient data centers, and optimizes operations across millions of customers to lower the per-unit cost of compute, storage, and networking. Those savings are then passed on to customers in the form of lower service prices. A concrete example is a small business getting access to enterprise-grade hardware and redundancy without the capital cost of building or maintaining it. This advantage is not just price; it also means broader product investments like managed services, security controls, and operational automation that would be costly for an individual company to replicate. A common misconception is thinking economies of scale guarantee the cheapest option for every workload; while base unit costs fall, specific high-performance or compliance-driven workloads may still require careful comparisons. When you build a TCO, include the implicit value of these shared investments: managed backups, global networking, and operational tooling. Ask yourself: which capabilities would be prohibitively expensive to develop in-house, and how does that change your migration calculus?

keyIdea.title: Shared savings
keyIdea.text: Large-scale providers spread fixed costs across many customers, lowering per-unit prices and enabling investments in managed features customers can leverage.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Economies of Scale
Benefit from massive economies of scale
Large providers lower per-unit costs and deliver managed services customers can’t economically build themselves.
Shared investments: hardware, power optimization, and operational automation reduce unit costs.
Access to enterprise-grade redundancy and features without building your own data centers.
Managed services like backups and databases reduce engineering overhead for customers.
Example

A small company gains access to resilient storage and managed snapshots without buying multiple redundant sites, because the provider spreads those infrastructure costs across many customers.

What to include in TCO
  • • Cost savings from pooled purchasing and lower power/hardware per unit.
  • • Value of managed services that otherwise require in-house engineering.
  • • Avoided capital and ongoing operational costs for redundancy and disaster recovery.
Misconception
Not every workload sees the same percentage of savings. High-compute or highly specialized systems may require tailored analysis, but many general workloads benefit substantially from shared infrastructure investments.

screens.title: Stop Guessing Capacity (Elasticity)
screens.subtitle: Right-size resources and scale dynamically to meet demand without waste

narration.text: Capacity planning on-premises forces organizations to make predictions and often over-provision for peak demand. AWS provides elasticity, which lets you provision exactly what you need and scale up or down as demand changes. Elasticity reduces wasted spend from idle servers and enables you to handle spikes without long procurement cycles. A practical example is an e-commerce site that experiences predictable traffic spikes during promotions; scaling instances or using managed auto-scaling ensures performance during peaks and lower cost the rest of the time. Elasticity is more than manual scaling — it includes autoscaling policies and serverless services that automatically adjust resources with demand. A common mistake is leaving resources running when they are no longer needed or failing to set scaling policies tied to meaningful metrics. In planning, include autoscaling settings, monitoring, and automation in your cost model. Think about which parts of your application need steady baseline capacity and which can be elastic; mixing reserved capacity for baseline and on-demand for spikes often gives the best cost-performance balance. Reflect: which of your systems can safely be made elastic to reduce cost and risk?

keyIdea.title: Elastic operations
keyIdea.text: Use autoscaling and serverless options to match capacity to demand so you only pay for what you use and avoid over‑provisioning.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Elasticity
Stop guessing capacity
Scale resources automatically to match demand and avoid wasted capacity.
Set autoscaling policies tied to metrics like CPU, request rate, or queue depth.
Combine reserved capacity for baseline needs and on-demand for spikes.
Use serverless functions to remove capacity planning entirely for bursty workloads.
Example scenario
An online sale causes 10x traffic. Autoscaling adds instances during the event and removes them afterward, avoiding both overload and long-term over-provisioning.
Scaling strategy cards
Baseline: Reserved capacity for predictable needs.
Burst: On-demand or serverless for unpredictable spikes.
Metrics: Define clear triggers to scale.
Automation: Use monitoring and policies to avoid manual errors.
Pitfall
Not configuring scaling policies or leaving long-running test resources active are common sources of unnecessary cost. Always include cleanup and monitoring as part of your plan.
Key Takeaway

Design for elasticity: baseline reservations plus on-demand scaling for bursts minimizes cost while meeting demand.

screens.title: Increase Speed and Agility
screens.subtitle: How quick provisioning and managed services enable faster experimentation and innovation

narration.text: Speed and agility come from the ability to provision resources quickly and to use managed services that reduce setup time. Traditionally, deploying new hardware, installing systems, and configuring networks can take weeks or months. On AWS you can provision thousands of servers in minutes, create managed databases, and use higher-level services to remove operational friction. This shortens the feedback loop for product teams and allows rapid experimentation. A concrete example is a development team spinning up a test environment to validate a prototype in hours rather than waiting for procurement. Speed reduces time-to-market and encourages iterative learning. A common misconception is that faster provisioning means less discipline; in reality, automation and infrastructure-as-code increase reproducibility and governance when applied correctly. When you evaluate migration benefits, quantify how quicker deployments translate to business outcomes like faster feature releases or reduced time for experiments. Consider also the operational benefit: engineers spend less time on undifferentiated tasks and more on building customer value. What small experiment could your team run this week if provisioning took minutes instead of months? Increase Speed and Agility means quick provisioning and managed services shorten development cycles and free teams to focus on product innovation rather than infrastructure setup.. In practical terms, how quick provisioning and managed services enable faster experimentation and innovation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Faster innovation
keyIdea.text: Quick provisioning and managed services shorten development cycles and free teams to focus on product innovation rather than infrastructure setup.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Speed & Agility
Increase speed and agility
Provision resources in minutes and use managed services to reduce setup time and operational burden.
• Rapid provisioning shortens feedback loops for product and platform teams.
• Managed services reduce setup and maintenance work, enabling focus on business logic.
• Infrastructure-as-code keeps faster provisioning reproducible and auditable.
Example
A team spins a test environment for a prototype in hours. That speed lets them try multiple designs, learn which yields better performance, and iterate more rapidly.
Practical guidance
  • • Use managed databases and storage to remove routine maintenance work.
  • • Automate provisioning with templates to keep speed repeatable and controlled.
  • • Measure experiment velocity: number of deploys or prototypes per quarter.
Key Takeaway

Speed alone isn’t the goal; speed paired with automation and governance increases safe experimentation and quicker business outcomes.

screens.title: Stop Spending Money Running Data Centers
screens.subtitle: How offloading infrastructure maintenance frees teams to work on differentiating projects

narration.text: Running data centers involves capital and operational costs: power, cooling, physical security, hardware refresh cycles, and staff time for maintenance. AWS takes responsibility for those base infrastructure tasks, allowing your teams to stop spending time and budget on undifferentiated heavy lifting. The concrete benefit is twofold: direct cost avoidance and opportunity cost reduction, because engineers can invest time in features that deliver customer value instead of routine maintenance. A common pitfall is assuming that offloading data center tasks removes all operational responsibility — you still manage application configuration, access controls, and your data. Effective cloud adoption reassigns staff time from physical infrastructure to cloud operations, automation, and product work. As you model TCO, subtract the facilities and hardware overhead and reallocate personnel costs to new cloud tasks. Think about which maintenance activities currently consume your team’s time and how those hours could be redirected toward innovation after migration. Stop Spending Money Running Data Centers means offloading base infrastructure reduces facilities costs and frees engineering time for product work, but operations responsibilities shift to cloud configuration and automation.. In practical terms, how offloading infrastructure maintenance frees teams to work on differentiating projects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Operational shift
keyIdea.text: Offloading base infrastructure reduces facilities costs and frees engineering time for product work, but operations responsibilities shift to cloud configuration and automation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › No Data Center Maintenance
Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers
Delegate facilities, hardware, and physical security to the provider and reassign team effort to product and cloud automation.
• Eliminate direct facility costs: power, cooling, and space.
• Avoid hardware refresh cycles and associated procurement burden.
• Reduce time spent on physical troubleshooting and hardware maintenance.
Example
A small operations team spends less time replacing failed drives and more time automating deployments and improving performance after migration.
Operational trade-offs
  • • Facilities and hardware tasks are eliminated, but cloud configuration and access control remain your responsibility.
  • • Measure time saved on maintenance and reassign to cloud engineering work.
  • • Ensure governance and automation to keep speed sustainable.
Key Takeaway

Moving away from data center maintenance frees resources for differentiation, but teams must adopt cloud best practices to manage their new responsibilities.

screens.title: Go Global in Minutes
screens.subtitle: Deploy applications across regions to reduce latency and meet data residency needs

narration.text: One of the powerful operational advantages of cloud providers is global infrastructure. Deploying to multiple regions gives lower latency to users, supports geographic redundancy, and helps meet data residency or compliance requirements without physically building your own data centers in each location. A simple example: replicating a web front end into another region can cut response times for distant users and improve resilience if a regional outage occurs. This geographic reach lets businesses expand internationally with lower upfront investment. A common pitfall is assuming global deployment is a single click without planning: you still need replication strategies, data synchronization, and considerations for regulatory compliance. When planning global deployments in a TCO, add costs for replicated storage, cross-region data transfer, and failover testing. Also identify which data must remain in a particular geography. Consider starting with a pilot region and measure latency and user experience improvements to justify the additional operational cost. Which markets would you prioritize for a pilot deployment and why? Go Global in Minutes means cloud regions let you deploy closer to customers and replicate services globally with lower capital investment, but you must plan for replication and compliance costs.. In practical terms, deploy applications across regions to reduce latency and meet data residency needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Global reach
keyIdea.text: Cloud regions let you deploy closer to customers and replicate services globally with lower capital investment, but you must plan for replication and compliance costs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Global Deployment
Go global in minutes
Use provider regions to place applications near users for performance and compliance.
• Deploy replicas to additional regions to lower latency.
• Use global load balancing and DNS routing to direct traffic.
• Consider data residency and compliance when replicating data.
Planning checklist
  • • Identify regions with the largest user base or regulatory need.
  • • Estimate cross-region data transfer and replicated storage costs.
  • • Plan for testing failover and measuring latency improvements.
Key Takeaway

Global reach removes the need to build physical data centers in each market, but operational planning and cost estimates for replication are essential.

screens.title: Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)
screens.subtitle: What to include when comparing on-premises to cloud, and how to frame qualitative benefits

narration.text: Total Cost of Ownership is a financial estimate that helps compare the direct and indirect costs of running a system on-premises versus in the cloud. For on-premises, include hardware procurement and amortization, software licenses, data center space and utilities, network infrastructure, IT staff time, maintenance, and backup and disaster recovery solutions. For AWS, include compute, storage, networking, managed service charges, and support plans. A crucial step is to include indirect costs and opportunity costs — for example, staff time freed from maintenance could be redeployed to new product features. Use a TCO calculator or a simple spreadsheet to map each on-premises category to an AWS equivalent, then show a multi-year view to account for hardware refresh cycles. A common mistake is forgetting staff time or operational overhead on either side of the comparison. Another is assuming all costs disappear when you move to cloud; some costs transform into recurring operational charges. When presenting a TCO, be explicit about assumptions such as utilization rates, discounting, and which services are managed versus self-managed. How would your assumptions about utilization change the projected savings?

keyIdea.title: TCO clarity
keyIdea.text: A complete TCO includes direct, indirect, and qualitative costs and transparently states assumptions about utilization and managed services.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Total Cost of Ownership
Understand TCO for cloud migration
Compare hardware, software, facilities, staff, and backup costs to equivalent cloud services and support.
• On-premises items: hardware amortization, licenses, data center, network, staff, backup.
• Cloud items: compute, storage, networking, managed services, support plans, and recurring operational fees.
• Include qualitative gains, like faster deployments and reduced maintenance.
A simple TCO exercise
On-premises annual costs:
  Hardware: $10,000
  Licenses: $2,000
  Data center: $5,000
  Staff (20%): $16,000
  Backup: $3,000
Map each to AWS services and estimate annual service charges for comparison.
Key Takeaway

Be specific about assumptions. Savings appear or disappear depending on utilization, managed services chosen, and which costs are included.

screens.title: Common Cost Pitfalls & Management Strategies
screens.subtitle: Avoiding unexpected bills and techniques to control cloud spending

narration.text: One common mistake is assuming cloud is always cheaper without careful planning. Unexpected costs arise from resources left running, over-provisioned services, inefficient storage choices, and cross-region data transfer. Another frequent issue is not using pricing options like reserved instances or savings plans for predictable workloads. To manage costs, adopt a culture of rightsizing, automation, and monitoring. Rightsizing means matching instance types and sizes to observed workloads. Automation ensures that non-production environments shut down when not in use. Monitoring and alerts surface unusual usage patterns that could signal runaway costs. Use tagging and chargeback mechanisms to allocate costs to teams, which encourages ownership of spending. A misconception to guard against is believing cost problems are only technical; often they are organizational. Policies, visibility, and governance are as important as technical optimizations. When you prepare a TCO or a cost plan, include time for ongoing cost management and automation. Which cost control would yield the largest predictable savings in your scenario: rightsizing, shutdown automation, or reserved pricing? Common Cost Pitfalls & Management Strategies means active cost management—rightsizing, automation, tagging, and using reservations—prevents surprises and captures savings from cloud consumption.. In practical terms, avoiding unexpected bills and techniques to control cloud spending. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cost control
keyIdea.text: Active cost management—rightsizing, automation, tagging, and using reservations—prevents surprises and captures savings from cloud consumption.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Cost Pitfalls
Common cost pitfalls
Unexpected charges usually come from unused resources, over-provisioning, and data-transfer or multi-region replication without planning.
• Leaving non-production resources running.
• Not rightsizing instances and storage classes.
• Forgetting to use reserved pricing for predictable workloads.
Management strategies
  • • Rightsize based on observed metrics.
  • • Automate shutdown of test/dev environments after hours.
  • • Use tags and reports for team-level accountability.
  • • Apply reserved or savings plans where usage is stable.
Common Mistake

Treating cost control as a one-time effort. It requires ongoing monitoring and governance tied to organizational processes.

screens.title: Shared Responsibility Model
screens.subtitle: What AWS secures for you and what you must secure in the cloud

narration.text: The Shared Responsibility Model clarifies which security tasks AWS performs and which ones remain your responsibility. AWS is responsible for the security of the cloud, meaning the underlying infrastructure: data centers, physical hosts, and foundational services. Customers are responsible for security in the cloud: their data, applications, operating systems, network configuration, access controls, and proper use of the services. A concrete example is that AWS maintains the physical security of servers, but you must configure firewalls, patch operating systems you manage, and protect credentials. A common misunderstanding is believing security is fully outsourced to the provider; in truth, misconfigurations and neglected updates on the customer side cause many vulnerabilities. When planning a migration, include security configuration, access control, monitoring, and compliance checks as operational tasks. Treat the model as a partner agreement: you benefit from the provider’s secure foundation, but you must design and operate the parts that run your workloads. What controls will you put in place to ensure your side of the responsibility is covered? Shared Responsibility Model means aws secures the physical infrastructure; you secure your data, configurations, access, and applications running on top of it.. In practical terms, what aws secures for you and what you must secure in the cloud. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Shared roles
keyIdea.text: AWS secures the physical infrastructure; you secure your data, configurations, access, and applications running on top of it.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Shared Responsibility
Shared Responsibility Model
Understand which security tasks are handled by the provider and which remain with you.
• Provider is responsible for the security of the cloud infrastructure and global facilities.
• You are responsible for security in the cloud: data, applications, OS, and access controls.
• Misconfigurations on the customer side are common causes of security incidents.
Operational checklist
  • • Configure network controls, access policies, and encryption.
  • • Patch managed operating systems and maintain backups.
  • • Monitor logs and set alerts for suspicious activity.
Misconception

Believing the cloud provider handles all security. In reality, many controls and configurations remain the customer's responsibility.

screens.title: Hands-on TCO Calculator Exercise (Conceptual)
screens.subtitle: Map the provided scenario to on-premises and AWS cost categories

narration.text: This exercise asks you to take a small scenario and list the cost categories on both the on-premises and AWS sides, then identify qualitative benefits. Start by listing on-premises items: hardware amortization, software licenses, data center space and utilities, staff time, and backup. Next, map each to likely AWS services: compute for instances, block or object storage, snapshots or managed backup, networking, and any managed database or support services. Use the provided annual figures to sketch a simple comparison. For example, hardware amortization of ten thousand dollars becomes a recurring instance charge; ten terabytes of storage maps to object or block storage fees; staff time moves from maintenance to cloud operations. Note where costs disappear entirely, such as physical data center utilities, and where they transform into operational charges. Also list qualitative benefits: faster provisioning, reduced maintenance, and global reach. A common error is forgetting to include staff transition costs and the ongoing cost of managed services. End by deciding which three categories most influence your estimate and why. This mental exercise prepares you to translate infrastructure into service-line costs for stakeholders.

keyIdea.title: Exercise outcome
keyIdea.text: You will be able to list on-premises and corresponding cloud cost categories, identify qualitative benefits, and prioritize the most influential assumptions.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › TCO Exercise
Scenario recap
5 physical servers (m5.large equivalent)
10 TB storage
IT staff 20% time
Annual costs:
  Hardware: $10,000
  Licenses: $2,000
  Data center: $5,000
  Staff (20%): $16,000
  Backup: $3,000
Step 1: List on-premises cost categories. Step 2: Map each to AWS service categories. Step 3: Identify three qualitative benefits to include in your presentation.
Mapping hints
  • • Hardware → Compute instances or managed compute services.
  • • Storage → Object or block storage and backup snapshots.
  • • Data center utilities → Eliminated, replaced by service fees.
  • • Staff time → Operational shift to cloud tasks; include transition time.
Key Takeaway

Walk stakeholders through assumptions and show how utilization and managed service choices change the numerical outcome.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact concept cards to keep in mind

narration.text: These are the core concepts to remember. First, Capital Expenditure versus Operational Expenditure: cloud shifts heavy upfront investments into recurring service costs, changing cash flow and risk. Second, Elasticity and avoiding capacity guessing: cloud lets you scale resources to demand so you pay for actual usage, but you must configure scaling and governance to capture savings. Third, Total Cost of Ownership and the Shared Responsibility Model: a TCO must include direct and indirect costs and state assumptions clearly, and security responsibilities are shared — AWS secures infrastructure while you secure your applications and data. Keep these three ideas visible when building a migration case: financial model, operational design, and security responsibilities. They together guide good decisions about where cloud will save money, where it requires governance, and where investments in automation deliver the most value.

keyIdea.title: Three reminders
keyIdea.text: Shift financial thinking to OpEx, design for elasticity, and include TCO and shared-security considerations in every migration plan.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Key Concepts
CapEx → OpEx
Shift from upfront hardware purchases to pay-for-use services that improve cash flow and reduce stranded assets.
Elasticity
Scale up or down to match demand and avoid over-provisioning; automation and monitoring are essential to capture value.
TCO & Shared Responsibility
Include direct and indirect costs in TCO and remember the security tasks you retain as the customer.
Summary
Use these three lenses—financial model, operational design, and security roles—when you recommend migration strategies and present TCO analysis to stakeholders.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three short definitions to anchor your understanding

narration.text: Keep these concise definitions handy. Capital Expenditure is upfront spending on physical assets like hardware and data centers, while Operational Expenditure is ongoing, pay-as-you-go costs for services consumed. Economies of Scale describe how large providers lower per-unit costs, enabling smaller customers to access advanced infrastructure. Elasticity is the ability to scale resources automatically to meet demand. The Shared Responsibility Model clarifies that while the provider secures the underlying infrastructure, you are responsible for your data and configuration. Use these definitions when building explanations for non-technical stakeholders to make migration decisions clearer and to justify assumptions in a TCO. A good next step is to take the scenario exercise and prepare a single-page slide showing costs, assumptions, and one qualitative benefit to present to a manager. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means short, precise definitions of capex/opex, economies of scale, elasticity, and shared security responsibilities to use when explaining cloud value.. In practical terms, three short definitions to anchor your understanding. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Short, precise definitions of CapEx/OpEx, economies of scale, elasticity, and shared security responsibilities to use when explaining cloud value.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Quick Reference
CapEx / OpEx
CapEx: upfront hardware spending. OpEx: ongoing, pay-as-you-go service charges.
Economies of Scale
Large-scale operations lower per-unit costs and enable shared investments in features.
Elasticity & TCO
Elasticity aligns cost with demand; TCO must list direct and indirect costs and state assumptions.
Final thought
Combine numeric TCO analysis with qualitative benefits to create a balanced migration recommendation that stakeholders can act on.
